extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (introductory sentential and predicate logic)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal rules for translating English into propositional formulas, building and using truth tables to analyze formulas and argument validity, and basic introduction to variables, sets, and truth sets in predicate notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine logical form by meaning, not word-for-word translation
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the logical form of a statement you must think about what the statement means, rather than just translating word by word into symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'but' often functions as 'and' when contrast is present; a forecaster saying 'Rain and snow are the only two possibilities' expresses a disjunction. Always parse the intended meaning before choosing connectives; literal word mappings can mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical connectives can be hidden in mathematical notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical relations can implicitly contain logical connectives (e.g., 3 < m2 expresses '3 < m or 3 = m'); multi-part inequalities (3 < a < 4) hide conjunctions and disjunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating mathematical expressions into propositional form, fill in the logical structure implied by the notation (e.g., 3 < a < 4 means (3 < a or 3 = a) and (a < 4)). You may sometimes omit single-letter abbreviations if the component statements are short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive-or is the default meaning of 'or' in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, 'or' always means inclusive or, unless specified otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus P v Q is true when P, Q, or both are true. If exclusive or is intended, it must be explicitly indicated (often by writing 'but not both' or using a special symbol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-table construction: list all combinations systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: A truth table lists each possible combination of truth values for the propositional letters; if a formula contains n different letters, its truth table must have 2^n rows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the rows systematically to avoid skipping possibilities. For multiple-letter formulas, compute intermediate columns stepwise from atomic letters up to more complex subformulas and the main connective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth rules for basic connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: How connectives determine truth values: P ∧ Q is true only if both P and Q are true; ¬P is true exactly when P is false; P ∨ Q (inclusive) is false only when both P and Q are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the basic truth tables (and, or, not) as building blocks for more complex formulas. The text provides the canonical tables and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main connective identification and stepwise evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: When computing a formula's truth values, work from atomic letters upward, identifying the main connective to obtain the final truth values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can make truth tables compactly by writing truth values under each connective symbol in the original formula and working outwards to the main connective. The main connective is the symbol under which the final truth values are listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument validity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument is valid if the premises cannot all be true without the conclusion being true as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth tables: include columns for each premise and the conclusion; if any row has all premises true and the conclusion false, the argument is invalid. The absence of such a row confirms validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using truth tables to test validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a truth table that lists truth values for each premise and the conclusion across all combinations of atomic sentences; inspect rows where all premises are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in every row where all premises are true the conclusion is also true, the argument is valid. Example walkthroughs show how a counterexample row demonstrates invalidity and reveals the source of the error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence determined by identical truth tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Two formulas are equivalent if they have the same truth value in every possible assignment of truth values (i.e., identical truth tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent formulas may be substituted for one another inside larger formulas. Use truth tables or known logical laws to verify equivalence (e.g., (¬S ∧ L) ∨ S equivalent to L ∨ S in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common logical equivalences and named laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of frequently used equivalences: DeMorgan's laws, commutative, associative, idempotent, distributive, absorption, double negation, and laws involving tautologies and contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these laws to simplify formulas and reason about equivalence. The text provides each law explicitly (e.g., ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q; P ∧ Q ≡ Q ∧ P; P ∨ (P ∧ Q) ≡ P; ¬¬P ≡ P).

rubrics_metrics.name: Associative law justifies omitting parentheses for same connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Because (P ∧ (Q ∧ R)) ≡ ((P ∧ Q) ∧ R) and similarly for ∨, parentheses may be omitted in formulas combining three or more statements with the same connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces clutter and avoids ambiguity when the connective is the same throughout; associative laws can extend to more than three statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tautology and contradiction definitions and laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A tautology is a formula always true (e.g., P ∨ ¬P); a contradiction is a formula always false (e.g., P ∧ ¬P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws: P ∧ (a tautology) ≡ P; P ∨ (a tautology) ≡ tautology; ¬(tautology) ≡ contradiction; P ∧ (contradiction) ≡ contradiction; P ∨ (contradiction) ≡ P; ¬(contradiction) ≡ tautology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use equivalences and laws to find simpler equivalent formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply DeMorgan's, double negation, distributive, idempotent, contradiction/tautology laws, etc., to transform complex formulas into simpler equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text show step-by-step transformations (e.g., ¬(P ∨ ¬Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ Q). Work through intermediate steps and justify each with a named law or truth table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact truth-table technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of separate columns for every subformula, list truth values under the corresponding connective symbols in the original formula and compute inward to the main connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method saves space and mirrors the formula's structure; the final truth values under the first (main) symbol give the formula's overall truth values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-formed formula (wff) awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every symbolic arrangement is a well-formed formula; wffs must obey formation rules (proper placement of connectives, parentheses, and atomic formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exercises that ask which expressions are wffs to practice recognizing syntactic correctness. (The text lists exercises asking to identify well-formed formulas.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Variables as predicates: P(x) notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use P(x) to denote a propositional statement about a variable x (e.g., P(x) = 'x is a prime number'), and use predicates with multiple arguments for relations (e.g., D(p,q) = 'p is divisible by q').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notation highlights dependence on variables and eases substitution: P(7) denotes the statement '7 is prime'. When multiple variables occur, list all variables in the predicate symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound vs free variables and renaming bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables inside set-builder or quantificational contexts may be bound (dummy variables) while others are free; bound variables can be renamed without changing meaning, free variables determine the truth-dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in y ∈ {x | x^2 < 9}, y is free and x is bound. Replace bound variable names (x → w) freely to avoid confusion. A statement with no free variables has a definite truth value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-builder (elementhood test) equivalence: y ∈ {x | P(x)} ↔ P(y)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement y ∈ {x | P(x)} means the same thing as P(y); the expression {x | P(x)} names a set and is not itself a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to convert between set membership statements and predicate statements; treat {x | ...} as binding the named variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth set definition for single-variable predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth set of a statement P(x) is the set of all values of x that make P(x) true; Truth set of P(x) = {x | P(x)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth sets to capture the values making a predicate true. This is defined for statements with one free variable; for multiple free variables see later chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify the universe of discourse (domain) for variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Free variables range over an understood universe of discourse; common choices include R, Q, Z, N (with notational conventions for positive/negative subsets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when necessary about the universe (e.g., 'x is a real number') to avoid ambiguity. The text lists common universes and notes conventions (e.g., whether 0 is in N).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explicit set definitions over ellipses to avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of defining large or infinite sets by a partial list with ellipses, give a defining property using set-builder notation (e.g., B = {x | x is a prime number}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids ambiguity about the intended continuation of a list and provides an unambiguous elementhood test for membership checks.
